newsitem.title: USA: Northeast Utilities eyes winter with calm.
newsitem.headline: Northeast Utilities eyes winter with calm.

text.p: Northeast Utilities (NU) said Friday it was confident of meeting its anticipated power demand of 5,300 megawatts (MW) this winter, by importing some 2,100 MW and taking additional measures.
The extra steps are necessary because NU's troubled nuclear plant operation remains shut down indefinitely.
"All things considered, we are in pretty good shape for the winter," NU spokesman Tom Shiel told Reuters in an interview.
"We're cautiously optimistic that we are going to be able to make it through the winter without any serious problems."
This is the first time since 1968 that NU has faced the prospect of winter without nuclear power.
NU's anticipated power demand during winter is 5,300 megawatts (MW), compared to 5,800 MW in summer, said Shiel.
"The Millstone (nuclear plants) closure had a great effect on our summer," said Shiel. NU added five more jet generators, of which four - at its Devon plant in Milford - will be available for winter.
In addition, NU will import up to 2,100 MW from outside Connecticut to bolster its power supply.
Its three Millstone nuclear plants in Waterford are shut down indefinitely because of safety concerns of federal regulators.
"It's predicted that at least one of the Millstone plants will be back in operation by the second half of 1997," said Shiel. "It's a question of whichever one is ready first."
In addition, NU's 28-year-old Connecticut Yankee nuclear plant in Haddam might be closed permanently, following its shutdown on July 22 of this year.
Connecticut Yankee's board of directors is expected to decide the plant's fate when it meets on December 4.
"There's a good possibility a decision will come out of that meeting," said Shiel.
When NU's nuclear plants were operational, it had total power generation of about 7,000 MW, including some that was exported.
But without Millstone and Connecticut Yankee, NU is losing 2,670 MW and 583 MW respectively.
"That leaves 3,747 MW available from Connecticut generation," said Shiel. "By reactivating some of our older units and adding the four new jets at Devon, we get 365 MW - and then we import 2,100 MW."
"Even if we hit the highest peak this winter, we should be able to weather the storm, because we do have a plan in place to deal with it," said Shiel.
He said the utility had made improvements to some of its systems and transmission lines ahead of the winter peak season.
